ai-system-design:0.prompt: In a RAG support chatbot, why are help-center articles split into chunks before embedding?
options: Embedding APIs reject documents longer than one sentence
Chunks retrieve focused passages that fit the context window, instead of whole long documents
Chunking encrypts the content
It removes the need for a vector index because each chunk can be matched with plain string search
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Smaller, coherent chunks give precise retrieval and let several relevant passages fit in the prompt. Embedding models accept far more than a sentence; the issue is relevance and context budget, not hard API limits.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Users ask about error code 'E-4012', but semantic (vector) search keeps returning generic troubleshooting articles. What is the best improvement?
options: Increase the LLM temperature
Switch to a larger chat model that has seen more error codes during training and can infer the fix
Remove chunk overlap
Add hybrid search: combine keyword/BM25 with vectors (e.g. via reciprocal rank fusion)
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Embeddings are weak at exact identifiers like codes and SKUs; lexical search excels there. Hybrid retrieval gets both. A bigger chat model can't fix retrieval that never surfaces the right document.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: What does a cross-encoder reranker add after initial vector retrieval?
options: It scores each (query, chunk) pair jointly to reorder the top candidates more accurately
It generates new documents to fill gaps when the retrieved chunks don't fully answer the question
It compresses embeddings to save storage
It translates queries into SQL
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Retrieve broadly (e.g. top 50) with cheap bi-encoder embeddings, then rerank with a more expensive model that reads query and chunk together, keeping the best few. It's a precision step, not generation or compression.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: A help article was updated yesterday, but the bot still quotes the old refund window. What's the most likely design gap?
options: The LLM's training data predates the update, so it keeps answering from what it memorised earlier
The vector DB has too many dimensions
The ingestion pipeline doesn't re-embed and replace chunks when source documents change
The system prompt is too short
ai-system-design:0.explanation: RAG answers come from indexed chunks; without change detection (updated_at, hashes, webhooks) and deletion of stale chunks, old content keeps being retrieved. Model training data matters less when answers are grounded in retrieval.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: When retrieval finds nothing relevant (all similarity scores are low), what should a support bot do?
options: Answer from the model's general knowledge, phrased confidently so the user isn't left without help
Say it doesn't know and offer escalation to a human agent
Return the top chunk anyway
Retry with temperature 1.0
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Grounded bots should refuse or escalate rather than hallucinate policy details. Returning low-relevance chunks or answering from general knowledge produces confident wrong answers about your product.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Why include source citations (article links/ids) in the bot's answers?
options: They let users and evaluators verify claims and make faithfulness easier to check
Providers charge less for cited answers
They make the model faster
They prevent prompt injection, because the model must stay consistent with the cited article text
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Citations make answers verifiable, build trust and let you measure groundedness. They don't affect cost or speed, and they don't stop injection, which needs separate defences.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Your bot serves multiple customers (tenants) from one vector index. Which design prevents Tenant A's docs from appearing in Tenant B's answers?
options: Tell the model in the system prompt to only use documents that belong to the current tenant's account
Use a different embedding model per tenant
Retrieve top-100 and hope the right tenant ranks first
Store tenant_id as metadata and enforce a filter (or namespace) on every retrieval query
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Isolation must be enforced at the data layer with filters or namespaces derived from the authenticated tenant. A prompt instruction can't un-leak data that has already been placed in context.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Chat history grows long and the model starts forgetting the user's order number from early in the conversation. What's a sound approach?
options: Truncate the oldest messages first and rely on the model to infer missing details from recent turns
Keep recent turns verbatim plus a running summary and key facts (e.g. order id) stored in state
Send only the latest message every time
Raise the temperature
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Combine a sliding window with summaries and structured memory for critical entities. Blind truncation or sending only the latest message loses exactly the context the user expects the bot to remember.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Which components belong in the offline ingestion side of a RAG chatbot? Select all that apply.
options: Parsing and cleaning source documents
Chunking and embedding text
Upserting vectors with metadata into the index
Streaming tokens to the user's browser
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Ingestion is the batch pipeline: parse, clean, chunk, embed, index. Streaming tokens is part of the online serving path at query time.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Which measures are sensible before launching the chatbot widely? Select all that apply.
options: An eval set of real support questions with expected answers
A human-handoff path for unresolved or sensitive issues
Removing logging to save storage
Tracking deflection rate and thumbs-up/down feedback
ai-system-design:0.explanation: Evals, escalation and outcome metrics are core to a support bot. Removing logging blinds you to failures; instead log with PII controls and retention policies.

ai-system-design:0.prompt: Embedding the user's query with a different embedding model than the one used for the document chunks still gives meaningful similarity scores.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:0.explanation: False. Different embedding models produce incompatible vector spaces (often different dimensions too). Queries and documents must use the same model; switching models requires re-embedding the corpus.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: What is the main purpose of an internal LLM gateway in front of multiple model providers?
options: To train custom models
To host the GPUs
To centralise routing, fallbacks, auth, rate limiting, cost tracking and logging behind one API
To replace the vector database by caching every embedding the providers return for each request
ai-system-design:1.explanation: A gateway gives every team one interface and enforces cross-cutting concerns: key management, quotas, failover, spend attribution, observability. It doesn't train or host models itself.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Provider A returns HTTP 429 for 2% of requests during peak. What should the gateway do first?
options: Retry the same request immediately in a tight loop until the provider accepts it, to keep latency low
Fail the request and alert the user to try later
Drop to a smaller context window
Back off exponentially with jitter (honouring Retry-After), then fall back to another provider
ai-system-design:1.explanation: 429 is a rate limit: back off with jitter, honour Retry-After, and fall back if the budget runs out. Tight retries amplify the overload (retry storm), and failing fast ignores a recoverable condition.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Why use a circuit breaker per provider in an LLM gateway?
options: It stops sending traffic to a failing provider for a cooldown, so requests fail over without waiting on timeouts
It splits long prompts into smaller pieces so that no single oversized request trips the provider's error threshold
It caches every response forever
It encrypts API keys at rest
ai-system-design:1.explanation: During an outage, every request otherwise waits for a timeout before falling back. An open circuit short-circuits to the fallback, then half-opens to probe recovery. It's a resilience pattern, not caching or encryption.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Rate limits for LLM APIs are often expressed in both requests per minute and tokens per minute. Why does the gateway need to track tokens, not just requests?
options: Tokens are cheaper to count than requests
A few huge prompts can exhaust the token quota while request counts look low
Providers ignore request counts entirely and only enforce limits on the number of tokens per day
Token limits only apply to streaming
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Request size varies by orders of magnitude, so a request-only limiter lets a handful of large calls blow the token budget. Estimate tokens before sending (and reconcile with actual usage) to enforce TPM limits.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: How should the gateway attribute LLM costs to teams and features?
options: Divide the monthly invoice equally across teams
Ask each team to estimate its usage quarterly
Record input/output token counts from each response with model, team and feature tags, priced by model
Count the number of requests per team, since every request costs about the same regardless of the model used
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Per-request usage metadata times per-model prices, tagged by caller, gives accurate attribution and lets you enforce budgets. Request counts ignore that output tokens and bigger models cost far more.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: You route easy queries to a small cheap model and hard ones to a large model. What's the main risk to manage?
options: Misrouting hard queries to the small model, degrading quality; validate the router with evals and allow escalation
The small model will refuse all requests
Large models tend to overthink easy queries and answer them less accurately, so all short queries must go to the small one
Routing makes caching impossible
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Cost routing saves money only if the classifier is accurate; misroutes hurt quality silently. Measure routed quality against an always-large baseline and add escalation (e.g. on low confidence or failed validation).

ai-system-design:1.prompt: A gateway falls back from Provider A to Provider B mid-request after A times out at 30s, then B also takes 30s. Users see 60s+ latency. What's the best fix?
options: Remove fallbacks entirely
Increase both timeouts to 60s so that slow responses complete instead of failing and triggering a fallback
Retry A three times before trying B
Set an overall deadline, shorter per-attempt timeouts (e.g. on time-to-first-token), or hedge requests
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Fallback chains need a total deadline so each attempt gets a slice; timing out on time-to-first-token detects stalls early. Longer timeouts or more retries make tail latency worse.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Which errors are generally reasonable to retry or fail over on in an LLM gateway? Select all that apply.
options: 429 Too Many Requests
503 Service Unavailable / provider overloaded
400 Bad Request due to an invalid parameter
Network timeout before any response
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Rate limits, overloads and timeouts are transient. A 400 means the request itself is wrong, so retrying the same payload fails again (though another provider may need a translated request).

ai-system-design:1.prompt: When falling back to a different provider, what can differ and must be handled by the gateway? Select all that apply.
options: Request/response formats for messages and tool calls
Context window limits
Output quality and behaviour on the same prompt
The HTTP status code for success always being 500
ai-system-design:1.explanation: Providers differ in API shape, limits and behaviour, so the gateway normalises formats, checks context fit, and fallback paths should be evaluated. Successful responses aren't 500s anywhere.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Streaming responses complicate fallback because once tokens have been sent to the client, switching providers mid-stream can produce duplicated or inconsistent output.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:1.explanation: True. Before the first token you can fail over transparently; after partial output, you must either abort and signal an error or restart clearly, since a new provider won't continue the exact same text.

ai-system-design:1.prompt: Storing provider API keys in the gateway and giving teams their own gateway credentials is worse for security than giving every team the raw provider keys.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:1.explanation: False. Centralising provider keys in the gateway lets you rotate them in one place and issue revocable, per-team credentials with quotas. Distributing raw keys widens the blast radius of any leak.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: How does a semantic cache differ from an exact-match cache for LLM responses?
options: It caches only images and other binary attachments, keyed by a perceptual hash of their content
It returns a cached answer when a new query's embedding is close enough to a past query's
It caches model weights in RAM
It stores responses only in the browser
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Semantic caches embed queries and look up nearest neighbours above a similarity threshold, so paraphrases can hit. Exact-match caches only hit on identical (normalised) prompts.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Your semantic cache returns the answer for 'How do I cancel my order?' when a user asks 'How do I not cancel my order?'. What's the most direct cause?
options: The similarity threshold is too permissive; near-identical embeddings can have opposite meanings
The cache TTL is too long
The LLM temperature is too high
The embedding dimension is too small to represent negation, so any two queries about cancelling collide in the index
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Embeddings of sentences that differ by a negation can be very close, so loose thresholds cause false hits. Tighten the threshold, evaluate on adversarial pairs, or verify hits. TTL controls staleness, not similarity errors.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Which kind of query is a poor fit for semantic caching?
options: 'What are your support hours?'
'What payment methods do you accept for orders?'
'What's the status of my order #8812?'
'How do I reset my password?'
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Personalised, user-specific or real-time answers must not be served from a shared cache; similar wording for different orders would leak or be wrong. Generic FAQs are ideal cache candidates.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: A semantic cache is shared across all users of a multi-tenant app. Which design flaw is most serious?
options: Cache entries use too much memory, so popular answers get evicted before they can be reused by other users
Cache keys aren't scoped by tenant, so one tenant's answer (with their data) can be served to another
The cache uses cosine similarity
Cache hits return faster than the LLM
ai-system-design:2.explanation: If answers depend on tenant data, cache keys must include tenant and access scope, or you leak data across customers. Cosine similarity and fast hits are expected behaviour.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Which signal best indicates your semantic cache threshold is set well?
options: Hit rate is around 99%, which shows the threshold is catching nearly every paraphrase in the traffic
The cache never misses
Embedding latency is below 1ms
On a labelled sample of hits, nearly all cached answers are correct, at an acceptable hit rate
ai-system-design:2.explanation: The trade-off is hit rate vs false-hit rate; you need precision measured on labelled hits. A 99% hit rate may simply mean the threshold is so loose that it serves wrong answers.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: The pricing policy in your help center changes. How should the semantic cache handle it?
options: Invalidate (or version) cache entries derived from affected documents, plus use TTLs as a safety net
Do nothing; similarity search will notice that the new documents have different embeddings and adapt
Lower the similarity threshold
Restart the LLM provider
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Cached answers embed old facts; tie entries to source document versions so updates invalidate them, and keep TTLs to bound staleness. Similarity search has no idea the underlying facts changed.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Besides semantic caching of full answers, which provider feature reduces cost and latency when many requests share a long identical prefix (e.g. a big system prompt)?
options: Higher temperature
Prompt (prefix) caching, which reuses computed state for repeated prompt prefixes
Shorter output limits, so the model reuses its previous answer instead of generating a long new one
Disabling streaming
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Prompt caching reuses the work for a stable prefix, so keep static content first and variable content last. It's distinct from semantic caching: the model still generates a fresh answer.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Which should be part of a semantic cache key or lookup filter? Select all that apply.
options: Tenant or user scope when answers depend on private data
Model and prompt-template version
Language/locale of the response
The current wall-clock second
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Scope, model/prompt version and locale all change what the correct cached answer is. Including the current second would make every key unique and the cache useless.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: What are the costs of adding a semantic cache in front of the LLM? Select all that apply.
options: An embedding call and vector lookup on every request, including misses
Risk of serving a wrong answer on a false hit
Invalidation complexity when source data changes
It makes the LLM's own answers less accurate on misses
ai-system-design:2.explanation: Misses pay extra latency for embedding + lookup, false hits hurt correctness, and invalidation is hard. On a miss the LLM is called normally, so its answer quality is unaffected.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: A semantic cache can serve a correct-looking answer even when the new question means something different from the cached one.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:2.explanation: True. Embedding similarity is approximate; queries with high similarity can differ in key details (dates, negation, product). That's why thresholds need tuning on real data and personalised queries should bypass the cache.

ai-system-design:2.prompt: Semantic caching is mainly useful when the workload has few repeated or paraphrased questions.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:2.explanation: False. It pays off when many users ask the same things in different words (FAQs, support). With mostly unique queries, you pay embedding and lookup costs for few hits.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Why is LLM inference token generation (decode) usually memory-bandwidth-bound rather than compute-bound at small batch sizes?
options: GPUs have no memory
Each token requires reading all the weights (and KV cache) from GPU memory, with little math per byte
Tokens are stored on disk
The CPU performs the matrix multiplications and has to copy every result back to the GPU after each step
ai-system-design:3.explanation: During decode, each step streams the full weights from HBM for one token per sequence, so arithmetic intensity is low. Batching more sequences reuses each weight read and improves utilisation.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: What does the KV cache store during autoregressive generation?
options: The attention keys and values for previous tokens, so they aren't recomputed for each new token
The final text of past conversations
A full copy of the model weights for each request, so concurrent users don't interfere with each other
Cached HTTP responses
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Each generated token attends over all previous tokens; caching their keys and values avoids recomputing them every step. It is per-request working memory, not a response cache.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: How does KV-cache memory scale for a single request?
options: It is constant regardless of length
It shrinks as generation proceeds
It grows roughly linearly with sequence length (prompt + generated tokens)
It grows with the square of the vocabulary size, since every token is compared to every other token
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Each token adds a fixed amount of keys/values per layer, so memory grows linearly with tokens, and multiplied across concurrent requests it often limits batch size. Attention compute, not KV memory, has the quadratic term.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: What is continuous (in-flight) batching in LLM serving?
options: Sending one request at a time to avoid contention
Waiting until exactly 32 requests have arrived, then processing them together as one fixed-size batch
Batching requests across different GPUs in different regions
Adding new requests to the running batch and removing finished ones at each decoding step
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Requests finish at different lengths; continuous batching refills freed slots every iteration, raising GPU utilisation and throughput. Static batching makes short requests wait for the longest in the batch.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Increasing batch size on an inference server generally has which effect?
options: Higher total throughput (tokens/s), but per-request latency can rise
Lower throughput and lower latency
No effect on throughput, because each request still gets the same share of GPU time per decode step
It reduces KV-cache memory per request to zero
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Bigger batches amortise weight reads across more sequences, boosting throughput, but each step does more work and queues may grow, increasing per-request latency. It's a classic throughput/latency trade-off.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Which two latency metrics matter most for a streaming chat UX?
options: Disk IOPS and DNS lookup time
Time to first token (TTFT) and inter-token latency / tokens per second
Model parameter count and vocabulary size
Embedding dimension and chunk size, since they decide how quickly the first chunk can be streamed
ai-system-design:3.explanation: TTFT drives perceived responsiveness (dominated by prefill and queueing), and inter-token latency drives reading smoothness. Parameter count influences these but isn't a user-facing latency metric.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: A self-hosted model serves fine at 10 concurrent users but runs out of GPU memory at 40 with long prompts. What is the most likely cause?
options: The tokenizer leaks memory
Too many HTTP connections
KV caches for 40 long sequences exceed remaining GPU memory after weights
The model weights are copied once per concurrent user, so memory grows with every new connection
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Weights are fixed; KV cache scales with concurrent sequences × length. Fixes: cap concurrency/context, paged KV-cache management, KV quantization, or more GPUs. HTTP connections are negligible.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Which techniques reduce GPU memory needed to serve an LLM? Select all that apply.
options: Quantizing weights (e.g. 8-bit or 4-bit)
Paged/efficient KV-cache allocation to reduce fragmentation
Sharing a common prompt prefix's KV cache across requests
Increasing the maximum context length
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Quantization shrinks weights, paged allocation wastes less KV memory, and prefix sharing avoids duplicate KV for common prefixes. A longer max context increases worst-case memory.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: What is true of the prefill phase compared with the decode phase? Select all that apply.
options: Prefill processes all prompt tokens in parallel
Prefill largely determines time to first token
Prefill tends to be compute-bound while decode is often memory-bound
Prefill generates one token per step sequentially
ai-system-design:3.explanation: Prefill runs the whole prompt through the model in parallel (compute-heavy) to produce the first token and build the KV cache. Sequential one-token-at-a-time generation is the decode phase.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Output tokens generally take longer to produce than the same number of input tokens take to process.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:3.explanation: True. Input tokens are processed in parallel during prefill, while output tokens are generated one step at a time. That's why long outputs dominate latency and providers usually price output tokens higher.

ai-system-design:3.prompt: Quantizing a model to fewer bits always has zero effect on output quality.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:3.explanation: False. Quantization trades some quality for memory and speed; moderate levels often lose little, but aggressive quantization can measurably degrade results. Evaluate on your own tasks.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Beyond standard HTTP metrics, what is most important to log for each LLM call in production?
options: Only the HTTP status code
Prompt version, model, token counts, latency (incl. TTFT), cost, and the request/response with PII controls
The user's IP address and user agent only, so abuse can be traced without ever storing prompt or response content
The GPU temperature at the provider
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Debugging LLM behaviour needs inputs, outputs, versions, token usage and timings tied to a trace. Status codes alone miss the main failure class: a 200 response with a wrong or harmful answer.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Why is tracing (spans per step) especially useful for RAG pipelines and agents?
options: It replaces the need for evals, since every bad answer can be spotted by reading the full trace by hand afterwards
It makes LLM calls faster
It shows each step (retrieval, rerank, LLM, tools) with inputs, outputs and timings, to locate failures
It encrypts prompts
ai-system-design:4.explanation: A wrong answer could come from retrieval, a tool, or generation; per-step spans reveal which. Traces complement evals, they don't replace them, and they add a little overhead rather than speed.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Error rate is 0% and p95 latency is fine, but users complain answers got worse after Tuesday's deploy. Which observability capability would catch this fastest?
options: CPU utilisation dashboards
Uptime pings and synthetic health checks hitting the chat endpoint every minute from several regions, alerting on failures
Database connection pool metrics
Online quality signals: feedback rates and sampled evals on live traffic, split by prompt/model version
ai-system-design:4.explanation: LLM regressions are usually quality failures with 200 OK responses. Tracking feedback and sampled eval scores by version shows the drop. Infrastructure metrics stay green when the model gives worse answers.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Your LLM bill doubled this week with no traffic increase. What should you look at first?
options: Token usage per request broken down by feature, model and prompt version, to find what grew
The number of Kubernetes pods running the API, since more pods means more parallel calls to the LLM provider
Disk space on the database
The front-end bundle size
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Cost scales with tokens × model price; a prompt change that adds context, a router sending more traffic to a bigger model, or an agent loop can double spend without more users. Infra metrics won't show it.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Why record a prompt-template version (or hash) with every LLM call?
options: Providers require it
It shrinks the token count
So quality, cost and latency changes can be attributed to specific prompt changes and rolled back
It prevents prompt injection, since the provider rejects requests whose template hash it does not recognise
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Prompts are code; versioning them in telemetry enables A/B comparison, regression detection and rollback. It doesn't affect tokens or security.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Storing full prompts and responses for every call raises what main concern, and what's the usual mitigation?
options: Slower model inference; use a faster model
Higher token costs, because logged prompts are re-sent to the provider; shorten prompts to compensate
Vendor lock-in; use multiple providers
Sensitive data in logs; redact PII, restrict access, set retention limits, and sample where possible
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Prompts often contain user PII and secrets; logs become a breach target and compliance issue. Redaction, access control, retention policies and sampling balance debuggability with privacy. Logging doesn't affect inference speed.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: An agent's p99 latency spiked to 90s while p50 is stable at 6s. Which trace analysis is most useful?
options: Compare slow traces' step counts and tool durations with typical ones to find loops or a slow dependency
Average all latencies into one number
Check only the first LLM call's latency
Look at the front-end console logs for slow renders that make the agent's answers appear late to the users
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Tail latency in agents usually comes from extra iterations, retries or a slow tool for a subset of requests. Comparing trace structure reveals it. Averages hide tails, and the first call alone misses later steps.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Which signals are useful online (production) quality indicators for an LLM feature? Select all that apply.
options: Thumbs-up/down and user corrections
Rate of escalation to a human or retry/regenerate clicks
Sampled LLM-as-judge or rule-based checks on live outputs
Number of lines of code in the prompt file
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Explicit feedback, implicit behaviour (regenerate, escalation) and sampled automated checks reveal quality. Prompt file length says nothing about answer quality.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: Which practices make LLM telemetry more actionable? Select all that apply.
options: Propagating a trace/request id through gateway, retrieval, LLM and tool calls
Tagging calls with feature, tenant and model
Logging only at the end of the request without step detail
Alerting on cost and token anomalies, not just errors
ai-system-design:4.explanation: Correlated ids, rich tags and anomaly alerts let you slice and spot problems early. End-only logs lose the per-step detail that's needed to debug multi-step pipelines.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: An LLM endpoint returning HTTP 200 for every request is good evidence that the feature is working correctly.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:4.explanation: False. Hallucinations, wrong tool choices, refusals and off-topic answers all return 200. LLM observability must include quality signals, not just availability.

ai-system-design:4.prompt: OpenTelemetry can be used to trace LLM calls alongside the rest of your backend services, and there are emerging semantic conventions for generative-AI spans.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:4.explanation: True. LLM calls are just spans in a distributed trace; OpenTelemetry has GenAI semantic conventions (model, token usage, etc.), so LLM telemetry can flow into your existing tracing backend.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Before sending support transcripts to a third-party LLM API, what is the most common technique to reduce PII exposure?
options: Compressing the text with gzip
Detecting and redacting/masking PII (names, emails, phones, card numbers) or swapping in placeholders
Translating the text into another language
Sending the text in multiple smaller requests so no single request contains a complete customer record
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Redaction or pseudonymisation removes identifiers before data leaves your boundary. Compression, translation and splitting all still transmit the raw PII to the provider.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: You replace emails with tokens like `<EMAIL_1>` before the LLM call and need the reply to address the user correctly. What's the right design?
options: Keep the mapping server-side per request and re-insert the real values into the response afterwards
Ask the LLM to guess the original email
Store the mapping in the prompt so the model can substitute the real values when it writes the final reply
Send the original email in a separate field to the provider
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Reversible pseudonymisation keeps the mapping in your system only, so the provider never sees the real value. Putting the mapping in the prompt or another field defeats the purpose.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Why are regex-only PII detectors insufficient for free-text chat?
options: Regex can't match email addresses
Regex is too slow to run on every message in production, so it adds unacceptable latency to each call
Regex patterns are illegal under GDPR
Names and addresses don't follow fixed patterns; combine regex with NER/ML-based detection
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Regex works well for structured data (emails, card numbers with Luhn checks), but names and addresses need entity recognition. Regex is fast and lawful; it just has poor recall on unstructured PII.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: A RAG system indexes HR documents. An employee asks the bot about a colleague's salary and gets the answer. What's the root design flaw?
options: The embedding model is too accurate, so it surfaces sensitive chunks that a weaker model would have missed
The chunk size is too small
Retrieval doesn't enforce the asking user's document-level permissions (ACL filtering)
The model temperature is too low
ai-system-design:5.explanation: RAG must respect source permissions: filter retrieved chunks by the user's access rights at query time. Otherwise the bot becomes a way around access controls. Embedding accuracy isn't the problem.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Which contractual/configuration check matters most when choosing an LLM provider for customer data?
options: Whether the provider's logo matches your brand
Data terms: training use of inputs, retention period, region, and a data processing agreement
Whether the API supports streaming, since streamed responses are never stored on the provider's servers
The number of models in their catalogue
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Privacy depends on what the provider does with your data: training use, retention, residency and DPA terms. Streaming support and catalogue size are product features, not privacy controls.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: A user exercises their right to deletion. Their chat logs were deleted, but answers about them still appear. What was most likely missed?
options: Derived copies: vector store chunks, caches and eval datasets built from their data
The user's browser cache
The provider's model weights were retrained on their chats and now memorise details about them
DNS records
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Deletion must cover every derived store: vector index entries, semantic caches, logs and eval sets. Vectors can leak content too. Model retraining is unlikely if the provider doesn't train on API data.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: What is the principle of data minimisation in an LLM feature?
options: Use the smallest model available, so less of the user's data can be memorised by the model weights
Compress all prompts
Delete the system prompt
Send the model only the data the task needs, and keep it only as long as necessary
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Minimisation limits exposure: don't stuff whole customer records into prompts when only the order status is needed, and limit retention. Model size is unrelated to privacy.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Which places can PII end up in an LLM application and need protection? Select all that apply.
options: Prompt/response logs and traces
Vector store chunks and embeddings
Semantic cache entries
The model provider's public status page
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Logs, vector stores and caches all persist user content. A provider's public status page doesn't contain your request data.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: An LLM could reveal PII in its output even if prompts are redacted. Which output-side controls help? Select all that apply.
options: Scanning responses for PII patterns before returning them
Restricting which documents/tools the model can access for this user
Raising the temperature to randomise output
Blocking or masking sensitive fields in tool results before they reach the model
ai-system-design:5.explanation: Output scanning, access scoping and masking tool results limit what the model can leak. Temperature changes randomness, not what sensitive data is available.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Embeddings are not a privacy concern because vectors are just numbers and the original text can never be recovered or inferred from them.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:5.explanation: False. Research shows text and attributes can be partially reconstructed or inferred from embeddings. Treat vector stores with the same protection, access controls and deletion obligations as the source data.

ai-system-design:5.prompt: Secrets such as database passwords or API keys should never be placed in prompts, because model output, logs and prompt injection can expose them.
options: True
False
ai-system-design:5.explanation: True. Anything in the context can be echoed back, logged or extracted via injection. Keep secrets in server-side tool executors, never in the model's context.
